en.content:
Hong Kong’s proposal to formalise the Chief Executive’s power to certify any criminal act as a national security case raises a question that goes beyond procedural detail: how to balance the need for safeguarding national security with the protection of legal certainty and the rights that underpin public trust. The government argues that clearer authority is necessary to respond decisively to security threats. Yet when discretion is expanded and made binding on courts, the public naturally worries about whether “national security” may be stretched to capture conduct that is already covered by ordinary criminal law, and whether defendants can meaningfully anticipate how their cases will be categorised from the outset.

A key challenge is not whether security threats exist—they clearly do—but how to ensure that the legal system remains predictable and proportionate. In any jurisdiction, the credibility of anti-subversion and anti-espionage efforts depends on restraint, transparency of standards, and the ability of courts and society to scrutinise decisions. If certification becomes, in effect, a gatekeeping mechanism that narrows judicial review, confidence may erode even among those who agree with the goal of defending national interests. The policy direction may be understandable, but it must be accompanied by safeguards that clarify thresholds, reduce ambiguity, and publish guidance so that enforcement is not perceived as politically elastic.

This editorial balance also matters because the same period’s local concerns—from public safety incidents on buses to broader social anxieties—show how quickly normal civic life can become entangled with wider governance questions. When citizens feel uncertain about where “ordinary crime” ends and “national security” begins, everyday institutions such as policing, prosecution, and sentencing can start to appear less about equal treatment under law and more about administrative discretion. In Hong Kong, where the rule-of-law tradition has long served as a stabilising social contract, reform that tightens security powers should therefore be judged not only by its intention, but by its effect on clarity, oversight, and due process.

Ultimately, Hong Kong can pursue strong national security without weakening the legitimacy of its legal framework. The government should state with greater precision the criteria for certification, outline how similar cases will be treated consistently, and—while respecting its mandate—ensure that procedural protections remain robust. Such measures would not undermine security; they would strengthen it by ensuring that enforcement is understood as lawful, measured, and credible, rather than open-ended.

zh.content:
香港近期一項法律修訂，建議由行政長官「認證」任何被視為相關的刑事行為，直接納入國家安全案件框架，並以法定形式約束司法判決。表面上，政府論述常以「明確程序、提升效率、確保威懾」作為理由，但核心問題其實係：當權力由立法與司法的制衡邏輯轉向更大幅度集中於行政主導，社會對公平審訊同時亦會更難預期。對市民而言，最關鍵唔係條文用咗咩形容詞，而係「證成」門檻同「認證」範圍一旦變得寬鬆，法律就可能由保障權利嘅工具，變成高度依賴政治判斷嘅通道。

更值得深思嘅，是國安語境下嘅「可裁量空間」會點樣擴張。若行政長官可以就某類行為作出定性，並令法院喺程序或適用上受限，法院仍能否充分發揮獨立審查角色，將成為制度風險所在。社會過去之所以對國安相關案件保持警惕，並唔係因為反對任何形式嘅法治或秩序，而係因為一旦「定性權」向行政集中，司法保障就可能出現結構性減弱：同一行為在不同個案、不同時間、不同政策風向下，結果難免變得較難被穩定理解。

不過，亦應承認：維護國家安全本身並唔等於要犧牲法治。真正可行嘅方向，應該係在「行政認證」之外，建立更可核查、更具透明度嘅制衡機制，例如界定更清晰嘅適用範圍、明確列出何謂「相關」、以及確保司法仍有充分空間就事實認定同法律適用作出獨立判斷。否則，制度就會沿住一條容易令人失望嘅路徑走：即使個案出於善意或良好意圖，長遠都會令市民對制度信任逐步折損，最後得益嘅唔係安全，反而係對社會共識嘅磨損。

我嘅立場係：政府可以談效率、談風險管理，但唔可以用「程序簡化」去換取「權力集中」而不付代價。香港最需要嘅，是能同時保護安全與保障權利嘅可預期法治，而唔係一套愈來愈難由公眾理解、亦較難由法院有效制衡嘅認證機制。當法律愈走向行政主導，社會就愈需要更高水平嘅透明度與更具體的限度，否則爭議會唔止停留喺新聞版面，而會滲入每一個普通人對司法公正的日常感受之中。
